pr_title: Add `-UnixTimeSeconds` to `Get-Date` to allow Unix time input
pr_body:
<!-- Anything that looks like this is a comment and can't be seen after the Pull Request is created. -->

# PR Summary

Add the `-UnixTimeSeconds` parameter to the `Get-Date` command.
This allows the time in seconds elapsed since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z (aka Unix Time).

PR #12179 has already been submitted, but my proposal is more like the specification proposed in #11719.
This proposal also supports negative values (meaning time before the Unix epoch), therefore improving compatibility with the [DateTimeOffset](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.datetimeoffset) class and the Linux `date` utility.

The following is an example of its use.

```powershell
> Get-Date -UnixTimeSeconds 1593696159

Thursday, July 2, 2020 1:22:39 PM

> Get-Date -UnixTimeSeconds -1

Wednesday, December 31, 1969 11:59:59 PM

```

The parameter has `-UnixTime` alias, because 'Unix Time' generally means a value expressed in seconds.
Also, consider the possibility of adding a parameter in the future that takes values expressed in milliseconds.

The parameter is named `UnixTimeSeconds`, not `FromUnixTime`.
This is for consistency with the `Date` parameter (it's not `FromDate`).

## PR Context

Close #12976

## Compatibility Notes
This proposal is basically compatible with PowerShell 7.0.2, but not compatible with 7.1.0-preview.4, including #12179.

It also includes a parameter set name changes. It's classified as Non-Public surface in the [guideline](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/blob/master/docs/dev-process/breaking-change-contract.md#bucket-4-clearly-non-public).

issue_context.title: Get-Date -FromUnixTime should support negative values.
issue_context.body:
## Summary of the new feature/enhancement

PR #12179 added FromUnixTime parameter to the Get-Date command.
In PowerShell 7.1.0-preview.3, the following command causes an error.

```
PS /> Get-Date -Date -1 -FromUnixTime
Get-Date: Cannot bind parameter 'Date'. Cannot convert value "-1" to type "System. DateTime". Error: "String '-1' was not recognized as a valid DateTime."
```

This command should support negative unix time.

On Ubuntu, the following commands will not return an error.

```
$ date --date "@-1"
Wed Dec 31 23:59:59 UTC 1969
```

## Proposed technical implementation details (optional)

The Date parameter of the Get-Date command has type [DateTime](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.datetime). If an integer value is passed for this parameter, it will be interpreted as [Ticks](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.datetime.ticks). This must be a positive value.

In other words, the following code is invalid.
```
PS /> [datetime] -1
InvalidArgument: Cannot convert value "-1" to type "System.DateTime". Error: "Ticks must be between DateTime.MinValue.Ticks and DateTime.MaxValue.Ticks. (Parameter 'ticks')"
```

Unix time can take a negative value, meaning that it is before Unix Epoch.

To allow the Date parameter to take a negative integer value, the type of this parameter must be changed to long.
But this is a breaking change.

I think the FromUnixTime parameter should be able to take a value, as was suggested in [#11719](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/issues/11719#issuecomment-581075598).
comments: We need to see real scenarios where the feature could be useful.
Rather than take the value in from `-Date` it almost seems better to just split the parameter set, and have `-FromUnixTime` take a value rather than be a switch parameter. 🤔

@vexx32  Agreed. BTW that's how I assumed it worked.  Because of positional binding, it "appears" to work that way:
```
PS. get-date -FromUnixTime 1242342344

Thursday, May 14, 2009 11:05:44 PM
```
What is a type of the parameter? Signed long?
Yeah, I think that makes the most sense. That does appear to have been the original proposal, too, but that didn't carry through to the initial implementation, it seems.

:tada:This issue was addressed in #13084, which has now been successfully released as `v7.1.0-preview.6`.:tada:

Handy links:
* [Release Notes](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/releases/tag/v7.1.0-preview.6)

review_comments: As an aside, @iSazonov: Do you know why `-AsUTC` cannot be combined with `-UFormat`? Was that intentional?
I think it can be in UFormat set too.

The AsUTC parameter can be combined with all other parameters.

In the [date](https://linux.die.net/man/1/date) command of Linux, if the -u parameter is specified, the date and time displayed in UTC, and if not, it's displayed in local time.

I mean why do you interpret `UnixTimeSeconds` as local Datetime here?
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.datetimeoffset.tounixtimeseconds?view=netcore-3.1#remarks

Because `dateToUse` is local time (it's not `DateTime.UtcNow`).

```cs
protected override void ProcessRecord()
{
    DateTime dateToUse = DateTime.Now;
```

This command consistently handles local time unless the `-AsUTC` parameter is set.

If the `-AsUTC` parameter is set, it will be handled by the code cited in the above comment, and therefore it has not been considered here.

I agree that outputting a local date by default makes sense with `-FromUnixTime` too, but to provide some background:

`Get-Date` _defaults to_ a local `[datetime]` instance (one whose `.Kind` property value is `Local`),  (`(Get-Date).Kind`) and you also get such an instance if you modify the current date with parameters such as `-Year`
 (e.g., `(Get-Date -Year 2019).Kind`).

By contrast, if you pass an argument to `-Date`:

* If you pass a _preexisting_ `[datetime]` instance, its `.Kind` property is retained (e.g.
`(Get-Date ([datetime]::UtcNow)).Kind` (`Utc`)

* If you pass a _string_ that is implicitly _converted to_ `[datetime]` _during parameter binding_ (that is, this logic is outside of `Get-Date`):
   * If that string _doesn't_ contain a time-zone offset, the `.Kind` property is `Unspecified`; e.g.,
 `(Get-Date 2020-01-01).Kind` (`Unspecified`) 
    * If it _does_ contain a time-zone offset (whatever it is, even if it indicates UTC), the `.Kind` property is `Local`; that is, _conversion to local time_ takes place; e.g., 
`(Get-Date 2020-01-01Z).Kind` (converted from UTC to `Local`).

With respect to string representations and `.ToUniversalTime()`, `Unspecified` instances behave like `Local` ones.
However, calling `.ToLocalTime()` on an `Unspecified` instance interprets it as _UTC_ time.
Ok, if we accept the default we should add a test and document this.

Hmm...

Would it be better to have `-Kind <DateTimeKind>` parameter instead of an `-AsUTC`?

I guess the DateTimeKind was added to mitigate Datetime type limitations (today we could use DateTimeOffset). I do not think that we should use DateTimeKind broadly. At least we could discuss this in new issue.

In fact, there already _is_ a proposal to implement this: #11731 - and I do think it makes perfect sense.

Whether or not we implement it as part of this PR, I think it's important to also include it in v7.1

I think a parameter like `-AsTimeZone PDT` would be useful.

Then I would also want features like `-FromTimeZone PDT -ToTimeZone JST`.

But adding those features to `Get-Date` would make the command overly complicated.
For example, I think we should add another command, such as `Convert-Time`.

Should there be a place for a comprehensive discussion on how `Get-Date` should handle timezone and offset-related parameters (including `-AsUTC`)?

@iSazonov: See my comment at https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/issues/11731#issuecomment-659279816.

I think that potential future `[datetimeoffset]` and time-zone (conversion) support should be discussed in a _new_ issue, which I encourage you, @aetos382, to create (as for the name `Convert-Time`: for consistency it's better to stick with the word "date").
@aetos382 You can open new issue to discuss Convert-Time/Date/Datetime cmdlet.
